subject: Geography
description: Plate tectonics, types of volcanoes, Ring of Fire, Richter scale, seismic waves

questions.stem: The 'RING OF FIRE' refers to a horseshoe-shaped zone of frequent volcanic + earthquake activity around the:

options.option_text: Atlantic Ocean rim, including Iceland and Brazil
Pacific Ocean rim, including Japan, Indonesia, Andes
Indian Ocean rim, including Madagascar and India
Arctic Ocean rim around the North Pole basin

questions.explanation: RING OF FIRE — ~40,000 km horseshoe around the Pacific Ocean. Hosts ~75% of world's active + dormant volcanoes and ~90% of earthquakes. Caused by SUBDUCTION at convergent plate boundaries — denser oceanic plates dive beneath continental plates → magma + earthquakes. Includes: Andes (S America), Cascades (US), Aleutian arc, Kamchatka, Japan, Philippines, Indonesia, NZ. Mt Fuji, Krakatoa, Vesuvius (no — Mediterranean), Mt St Helens, Pinatubo all here. Indian Ocean has fewer such margins (mostly mid-ocean spreading + the Sunda subduction zone in the east — where 2004 tsunami quake occurred).
questions.subject: Geography

options.option_text: Damage caused at the surface to buildings
Magnitude (energy released) on a logarithmic scale
Frequency in a region per unit time interval
Depth at which the seismic event occurred underground

questions.explanation: Richter scale — measures MAGNITUDE (energy released at the source). LOGARITHMIC: each whole number is 10× the amplitude and ~32× the energy. Magnitude 7 quake releases ~32× more energy than magnitude 6. Devised by Charles Richter (1935) for southern California. Modern seismologists use the MOMENT MAGNITUDE SCALE (M_w) for large quakes (Richter saturates above ~7). MERCALLI scale (Distractor 1) — measures intensity / observed effects (1-12 Roman numerals); subjective. Distractors 3, 4 are different parameters.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The point INSIDE the earth where an earthquake originates is called the:

options.option_text: Epicentre, the location directly above the source
Focus or hypocentre, the actual subterranean origin
Magnitude reading observed on the recorder
Tsunami zone of inundation along coasts

questions.explanation: FOCUS / HYPOCENTRE — the actual underground point of energy release. EPICENTRE — point on Earth's surface directly ABOVE the focus (where shaking is usually most intense). Quake depth classification: SHALLOW (< 70 km) — most damaging, most common; INTERMEDIATE (70-300 km); DEEP (> 300 km) — usually felt little at surface, occur in subduction zones. Distractor 1 wrongly defines focus as epicentre. Distractors 3, 4 are unrelated terms.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The INDIA's only ACTIVE volcano is:

options.option_text: Mt Abu in Rajasthan, of the Aravalli range
Barren Island in the Andaman Sea, off mainland
Mt Girnar in Gujarat, of religious significance
Mt Mahendragiri of Tamil Nadu hill ranges

questions.explanation: BARREN ISLAND — in the Andaman Sea, ~135 km NE of Port Blair. Only active volcano in India. Stratovolcano on the Burma microplate at the Sunda subduction. Erupted multiple times — most recently 2017, 2018, 2022 (small). NARCONDAM ISLAND nearby — DORMANT volcano. Mt Abu (Rajasthan) — Aravalli highland, NOT volcanic. Mt Girnar (Gujarat) — Junagadh, granitic intrusion (~250 Ma old), highly eroded, sacred but not active. Distractor 4 — Tamil Nadu mountains aren't volcanic.
questions.subject: Geography

options.option_text: The rotation of the Earth speeding up over time
Sudden release of stored elastic energy along faults
The Moon's gravitational pull as the tides change
Atmospheric pressure changes during major storms

questions.explanation: Plate tectonics — plates move slowly (~few cm/yr); friction at boundaries means stress builds up over decades-centuries. When stress exceeds rock strength → SUDDEN slip along a FAULT line → earthquake. Energy radiated as SEISMIC WAVES (P-waves: primary, faster, longitudinal; S-waves: secondary, slower, transverse; Surface waves — most damaging). Most quakes occur at plate boundaries (transform — San Andreas, convergent — Himalayas, divergent — mid-Atlantic ridge). Distractor 3 — tidal forces affect Earth but don't drive quakes. Distractor 4 — atmospheric effects negligible.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: VOLCANIC ERUPTIONS contribute to soil fertility because:

options.option_text: Lava cools to form solid bedrock that nourishes plants
Volcanic ash + lava weather to release minerals beneficial to soil
Volcanic gases like SO₂ are good plant fertilisers
Heat from eruptions sterilises the soil for new growth

questions.explanation: Volcanic ash + weathered lava (basalt) release minerals (Ca, Mg, K, P, micronutrients) → among the most fertile soils on Earth. Examples: Java (Indonesia) — densely populated and farmed despite frequent eruptions; Italy — Campania near Vesuvius famed for tomato + lemon production; Mt Etna's slopes — vineyards, citrus. India: Deccan basalt soils give rise to BLACK COTTON SOIL (regur) — high water-holding capacity, famous for cotton cultivation. Distractor 1 — fresh bedrock isn't fertile until weathered. Distractor 3 — SO₂ is harmful, not a fertiliser. Distractor 4 — sterilisation is harmful, not beneficial.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The 2004 BOXING DAY TSUNAMI was triggered by an earthquake near the coast of:

options.option_text: Japan, the Tohoku coast in the Pacific Ocean
Sumatra in Indonesia, in the Indian Ocean
California coast along the San Andreas fault
Chile coast in the Pacific Ring of Fire

questions.explanation: 26 December 2004 — Mw 9.1-9.3 megathrust earthquake near SUMATRA, Indonesia (Indian Ocean). 3rd largest ever recorded. Triggered tsunami waves up to 30 m → killed ~230,000 across 14 countries (Indonesia worst — Aceh; then Sri Lanka, India — TN coast, Andaman/Nicobar, Thailand, Maldives, even African coasts). India set up Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System after this disaster (operational since 2007, INCOIS Hyderabad). 2011 TŌHOKU earthquake (Japan, Mw 9.1) caused Fukushima nuclear disaster. 1960 Valdivia (Chile, Mw 9.5) — largest ever recorded.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which type of seismic body wave cannot travel through Earth's liquid outer core, a property that first revealed the outer core is molten?

options.option_text: P-waves (Primary compressional waves, travel through solids and liquids)
S-waves (Secondary shear waves, can only propagate through solid media)
Love waves (horizontal surface waves, confined to Earth's uppermost crust)
Rayleigh waves (rolling surface waves that move like deep ocean waves)

questions.explanation: S-waves (shear waves) require a rigid medium to transfer energy; they cannot propagate through liquids. When S-waves were observed to vanish beyond ~105° from an earthquake's epicentre, seismologists deduced that Earth's outer core must be liquid. P-waves (Option A) travel through both solids and liquids and do pass through the outer core, which is why they are not blocked.

questions.stem: When the roof of a magma chamber collapses inward after a massive volcanic eruption drains the chamber, the broad basin-shaped depression that forms is termed a?

options.option_text: Crater — the relatively small vent opening at a volcano's summit
Fumarole — a crack in the ground that emits volcanic gases and steam
Caldera — a broad collapse depression above an emptied magma chamber
Lahar — a volcanic mudflow or debris flow descending a volcanic slope

questions.explanation: A caldera (from Spanish for 'cauldron') forms when the overlying rock collapses into the void left by an evacuated magma chamber — it can be kilometres wide. Yellowstone and Toba are classic calderas. Option A (crater) is the comparatively small opening through which lava and gases vent; it forms by explosion or normal eruption, not chamber collapse.

questions.stem: The fast-moving current of superheated gas and volcanic fragments that swept down Mt. Vesuvius and buried the Roman city of Pompeii in 79 CE is classified in volcanology as a?

options.option_text: Lahar — a volcanic mudflow that carries ash and pyroclastic debris
Pyroclastic flow — a dense, hot mixture of gas and fragmented volcanic matter
Lava tube — an underground channel formed by crusting basaltic lava flow
Tephra column — vertical suspension of volcanic ash and cinder in the air

questions.explanation: Pyroclastic flows (also called nuée ardente) can exceed 700 °C and travel at over 100 km/h, leaving victims instantly asphyxiated — which is exactly what the casts at Pompeii reveal. Option A (lahar) requires water mixing with volcanic material; Option C (lava tube) is a solid structural feature, not a destructive current.

questions.stem: The Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale is fundamentally different from the Richter scale because MMI measures earthquake?

options.option_text: Total energy released at the earthquake's subsurface focus point
Amplitude of seismic waves as recorded on a calibrated seismograph
Perceived shaking and visible structural damage observed at the surface
Depth of the hypocentre below the Earth's surface measured in kilometres

questions.explanation: MMI is an intensity scale — it grades what people feel and what damage buildings suffer (I = not felt; XII = total destruction). The Richter scale (and its successor, the Moment Magnitude Scale Mw) measures the magnitude, i.e., energy released, objectively from instrument recordings. The same magnitude earthquake can produce very different MMI values depending on soil type and distance from the epicentre.

questions.stem: Although P-waves arrive first at a seismic station and S-waves arrive second, the greatest structural damage to surface buildings during an earthquake is usually caused by?

options.option_text: P-waves, as they travel fastest and compress structures along their path
S-waves, because their vertical motion directly undermines building foundations
Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh), which carry the largest displacement amplitude
Deep-focus body waves originating below the Mohorovičić discontinuity layer

questions.explanation: Surface waves (Love waves shear horizontally; Rayleigh waves roll like ocean swells) arrive last but carry the most energy amplitude at the surface, making them the primary agents of building collapse. P-waves and S-waves (body waves) attenuate more rapidly with distance. Option D is a distractor — deep-focus earthquakes actually produce weaker surface shaking than shallow-focus quakes.

questions.stem: During the 1964 Alaska (Good Friday) earthquake, saturated sandy soil in coastal areas suddenly lost cohesion and flowed like a viscous liquid, causing buildings to sink and tilt — this geotechnical hazard is called?

options.option_text: Soil creep — very slow downslope movement of soil under gravitational pull
Seismic amplification — increase in shaking intensity across soft sediment layers
Soil liquefaction — fluid-like behaviour of saturated granular soil during shaking
Thixotropy — reversible gel-to-sol transformation observed in colloidal clay soils

questions.explanation: Liquefaction occurs when cyclic seismic shaking increases pore-water pressure in saturated, loosely packed granular soil until effective stress drops to zero — the soil temporarily behaves like a liquid. It caused enormous damage in Anchorage in 1964 and in Christchurch (2010–11). Option B (seismic amplification) increases shaking intensity but does not turn solid ground into liquid; Option D (thixotropy) is a colloidal property unrelated to seismically induced failure.

questions.stem: Deep-focus earthquakes (hypocentre 300–700 km) are restricted to subduction zones. The inclined plane within a descending slab where these quakes cluster is named after which pair of seismologists?

options.option_text: Alfred Wegener — proposer of continental drift and seafloor spreading theory
Andrija Mohorovičić — discoverer of the seismic crust-mantle discontinuity
Hugo Benioff and Kiyoo Wadati — the seismologists who mapped this seismic zone
Charles Richter — who devised the logarithmic seismic magnitude scale in 1935

questions.explanation: The Wadati-Benioff zone (also called the Benioff zone) is the dipping plane of seismicity that traces a subducting oceanic slab as it plunges into the mantle. Japanese seismologist Kiyoo Wadati described it in 1928 and American Hugo Benioff independently detailed it in the 1940s. Option B (Mohorovičić) discovered the crust-mantle boundary (Moho) but not this subduction-related seismic plane. Deep-focus earthquakes here are the only earthquakes below ~300 km.
